summary.text: For any odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\) with \(p<n\), Fermat’s theorem makes the factors indexed by multiples of \(p-1\) supply more powers of \(p\) than occur in \((n-1)!\), so \(p\mid a(n-1)\), contradicting the hypothesis; hence a composite \(n\) would be \(2^t\), but \(v_2(a(2^t-1))=t-1\) (using \(v_2((2^t-1)!)=2^t-1-t\)) contradicts the required divisibility by \(2^t\). Once \(n\) is prime, if the order \(d\) of \(2\bmod n\) were less than \(n-1\), the factor \(2^d-1\) in the defining product would force \(n\mid a(n-1)\), and thus \(n\mid2^{n-2}\), impossible; therefore \(d=n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(m)=\frac{2^{m-1}}{m!}\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(2^i-1)\qquad(m\ge 1).
\]
We first establish that this quotient is an integer and record the divisibility information about it that will be needed later.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We use the following standard recurrence for factorial valuations. If \(s=pu+r\), where \(0\le r<p\), then
\[
v_p(s!)=u+v_p(u!). \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, among \(1,2,\ldots,pu+r\), the multiples of \(p\) are exactly
\(p,2p,\ldots,up\). They contribute one factor of \(p\) each, and their additional factors of \(p\) are precisely those occurring in \(1,2,\ldots,u\).

A consequence that we will repeatedly use is
\[
(p-1)v_p(s!)<s \qquad(s>0). \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, this follows by strong induction on \(s\). Write \(s=pu+r\), \(0\le r<p\). If \(u=0\), then \(s<p\), so \(v_p(s!)=0<s\). If \(u>0\), (1) and the induction hypothesis give
\[
(p-1)v_p(s!)=(p-1)u+(p-1)v_p(u!)
<(p-1)u+u=pu\le pu+r=s.
\]

We now prove the integrality of \(A(m)\). Put
\[
N_m=2^{m-1}\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(2^i-1).
\]
It is enough to prove, for every prime \(p\), that
\(p^{v_p(m!)}\mid N_m\).

For \(p=2\), (2) says \(v_2(m!)<m\), and hence
\(v_2(m!)\le m-1\). Thus the required power of \(2\) divides the factor \(2^{m-1}\).

Now let \(p\) be odd and put \(k=v_p(m!)\). By (2),
\[
k(p-1)<m.
\]
For each \(j=1,\ldots,k\), the index \(j(p-1)\) therefore lies between \(1\) and \(m-1\). Fermat's theorem gives
\[
p\mid 2^{p-1}-1.
\]
Since \(p-1\mid j(p-1)\), the elementary factorization
\(x^a-1\mid x^b-1\) whenever \(a\mid b\) shows that
\[
p\mid 2^{j(p-1)}-1.
\]
These are \(k\) distinct factors in the product defining \(N_m\), so their product is divisible by \(p^k\). Hence every prime power occurring in \(m!\) divides \(N_m\), and consequently
\[
m!\mid N_m. \tag{3}
\]
Thus \(A(m)=N_m/m!\) is indeed an integer.

We need a strengthened version of the odd-prime part of this argument. If \(p\) is odd and
\[
\bigl(v_p(m!)+1\bigr)(p-1)<m, \tag{4}
\]
then the factors with indices
\[
p-1,\ 2(p-1),\ldots,\bigl(v_p(m!)+1\bigr)(p-1)
\]
show that \(p^{v_p(m!)+1}\mid N_m\). Since \(m!\mid N_m\), cancellation of the exact \(p\)-power in \(m!\) gives
\[
p\mid A(m). \tag{5}
\]

We next derive the estimate that will make (4) applicable to a proper odd prime divisor of a composite number. Suppose \(p\) is prime, \(p\mid n\), and \(n\ne p\). Write
\[
n=pq.
\]
Because \(n>0\), we have \(q>0\); because \(n\ne p\), we have \(q\ne1\), so \(q\ge2\). We can write
\[
n-1=p(q-1)+(p-1).
\]
Applying (1), with quotient \(q-1\) and remainder \(p-1<p\), gives
\[
v_p((n-1)!)=(q-1)+v_p((q-1)!). \tag{6}
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl(v_p((n-1)!)+1\bigr)(p-1)
 &=\bigl(q+v_p((q-1)!)\bigr)(p-1)\\
 &=q(p-1)+(p-1)v_p((q-1)!).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (2), applied to \(q-1>0\),
\[
(p-1)v_p((q-1)!)<q-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
\bigl(v_p((n-1)!)+1\bigr)(p-1)
<q(p-1)+(q-1)=pq-1=n-1. \tag{7}
\]
In particular, if \(p\) is an odd prime divisor of \(n\) and \(n\ne p\), then (5), with \(m=n-1\), yields
\[
p\mid A(n-1). \tag{8}
\]

Now assume \(n>2\) and
\[
n\mid A(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{9}
\]
We first prove that \(n\) is prime.

Let \(p\) be any odd prime divisor of \(n\). We claim that necessarily \(n=p\). If not, (8) gives \(p\mid A(n-1)\). Since \(p\mid n\), hypothesis (9) also gives
\[
p\mid A(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting the first divisibility from the second gives
\[
p\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
As \(p\) is prime, this implies \(p\mid2\), which is impossible for an odd prime. Thus every odd prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\) must satisfy \(n=p\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(n\) is not prime. The preceding conclusion then implies that \(n\) has no odd prime divisor: if it had one, \(n\) would equal that prime and hence would be prime. By unique factorization, a positive integer with no prime divisor other than \(2\) is a power of \(2\). Hence
\[
n=2^t
\]
for some integer \(t\ge0\). Since \(n>2\), in fact \(t\ge2\).

We now compute the exact \(2\)-adic valuation of \(A(2^t-1)\). First,
\[
v_2\bigl((2^t-1)!\bigr)=2^t-1-t. \tag{10}
\]
This can be proved directly by induction on \(t\). It is clear for \(t=0\). If it holds for \(t\), observe that
\[
2^{t+1}-1=2(2^t-1)+1.
\]
Using recurrence (1) for \(p=2\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2\bigl((2^{t+1}-1)!\bigr)
 &= (2^t-1)+v_2\bigl((2^t-1)!\bigr)\\
 &= (2^t-1)+(2^t-1-t)\\
 &=2^{t+1}-1-(t+1),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (10).

Set \(m=2^t-1\). Every factor \(2^i-1\) in
\(\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(2^i-1)\) is odd. Thus the entire \(2\)-adic valuation of the numerator \(N_m\) comes from \(2^{m-1}\), and is
\[
v_2(N_m)=m-1=2^t-2.
\]
Using (3) and (10), the valuation of the exact quotient is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2(A(2^t-1))
 &=v_2(N_m)-v_2(m!)\\
 &=(2^t-2)-(2^t-1-t)\\
 &=t-1. \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(t\ge2\), one has
\[
t\le 2^t-2. \tag{12}
\]
This follows, for example, by induction starting with equality at \(t=2\). Hence
\[
2^t\mid 2^{2^t-2}.
\]
Substituting \(n=2^t\) into (9) gives
\[
2^t\mid A(2^t-1)+2^{2^t-2}.
\]
Since the second summand is divisible by \(2^t\), it follows that
\[
2^t\mid A(2^t-1).
\]
This says that \(v_2(A(2^t-1))\ge t\), contradicting the exact value \(t-1\) in (11). Thus \(n\) cannot be composite. We have proved that \(n\) is prime.

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Since \(n>2\) is prime, \(2\not\equiv0\pmod n\), so \(2\) is an element of the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times\). Let
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)
\]
be its multiplicative order. This group has \(n-1\) elements, so Lagrange's theorem gives
\[
d\mid n-1. \tag{13}
\]
In particular \(1\le d\le n-1\).

We show that equality must hold. Suppose instead that \(d<n-1\). By the definition of order,
\[
2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
n\mid 2^d-1. \tag{14}
\]
Because \(1\le d<n-1\), the factor \(2^d-1\) occurs in
\[
P=\prod_{i=1}^{n-2}(2^i-1).
\]
Consequently (14) implies \(n\mid P\), and hence
\[
n\mid N_{n-1}=2^{n-2}P. \tag{15}
\]
On the other hand, by the integrality result (3),
\[
N_{n-1}=(n-1)!\,A(n-1). \tag{16}
\]
Since \(n\) is prime and all factors of \((n-1)!\) are smaller than \(n\), we have
\(n\nmid(n-1)!\). From (15), (16), and Euclid's lemma for the prime \(n\), it follows that
\[
n\mid A(n-1). \tag{17}
\]
Combining (17) with the original hypothesis (9), we obtain
\[
n\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
Because \(n\) is prime, this forces \(n\mid2\), and therefore \(n\le2\), contrary to \(n>2\). This contradiction proves
\[
d=n-1.
\]
Finally, for a prime \(n\), Euler's totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Hence the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) is \(\varphi(n)\), exactly the assertion that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Therefore, for every integer \(n>2\), if
\[
n\mid A(n-1)+2^{n-2},
\]
then \(n\) is prime and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).
